cse-2005-cs-24.approach: ARP maps a known network-layer (IP) address to the unknown link-layer (MAC) address on the same LAN, by broadcasting a request and receiving a unicast reply.

steps.title: What ARP resolves
steps.body: A host knows the next-hop **IP address** but must put a **MAC address** into the Ethernet frame. It broadcasts "Who has IP $x$?" and the owner replies with its MAC address.

steps.title: Direction of the mapping
steps.body: IP $\to$ MAC. The reverse direction (MAC $\to$ IP) is RARP/BOOTP/DHCP; name $\to$ IP is DNS.

answer.value: Finding the MAC address that corresponds to an IP address

The gateway IP is configured (or given by DHCP); ARP is then used to find the gateway's *MAC*, not its IP.
This is the reverse mapping (MAC → IP), done by RARP/DHCP.
Exactly what ARP does: IP address → MAC address on the local link.

pitfalls: Do not confuse ARP (IP→MAC) with RARP (MAC→IP).

cse-2005-cs-25.approach: With $n$-bit sequence numbers there are $2^n$ numbers; in selective repeat the sender and receiver windows must not overlap after a wrap-around, so each window can be at most half the sequence space.

steps.title: Constraint
steps.body: With send window $W_s$ and receive window $W_r$, selective repeat needs $W_s + W_r \le 2^n$, otherwise a retransmitted old frame can be mistaken for a new one. With $W_s = W_r = W$: $2W \le 2^n \Rightarrow W \le 2^{n-1}$.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: $n = 3$: 8 sequence numbers, window $\le 4$. With window 5, if all ACKs of frames 0–4 are lost, the receiver now expects 5,6,7,0,1 and would accept the retransmitted old frame 0 as new.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^n$ is the whole sequence space — windows would fully overlap; not even Go-Back-N allows this.
Correct: $W \le 2^n/2 = 2^{n-1}$.
$2^n-1$ is the Go-Back-N limit (receiver window 1), not selective repeat.
$2^{n-2}$ is safe but not the maximum.

cse-2005-cs-25.verification: Checked with n = 3: window 4 works, window 5 fails when ACKs are lost.

cse-2005-cs-26.approach: Transparent bridges flood frames to unknown destinations; if the bridged LANs contain a cycle, frames circulate forever. The spanning tree algorithm disables redundant ports so the active topology is a loop-free tree.

steps.title: Problem with cycles
steps.body: A broadcast or unknown-destination frame is forwarded on every port; in a cyclic topology copies come back and are forwarded again (broadcast storm), and address-learning tables oscillate.

steps.title: What the spanning tree does
steps.body: Bridges elect a root and keep only the ports on a spanning tree of the LAN graph active. A tree has exactly one path between any two LANs, so loops are impossible.

answer.value: For avoiding loops in the routing paths

optionAnalysis.reason: The tree paths are not necessarily shortest between two LANs — only toward the root is cost minimised.
Correct: a spanning tree has no cycles, so frames cannot loop.
Redundant links are *blocked*; fault tolerance is only a side benefit (re-computation after failure), not the reason.
Collisions are confined within a LAN segment by bridges anyway; STP has nothing to do with them.

cse-2005-cs-26.verification: IEEE 802.1D: the purpose of STP is a loop-free active topology.

cse-2005-cs-28.approach: Indexes live on disk and the cost of a lookup is the number of block transfers. A B+-tree packs many keys in a node sized to a disk block, giving a very high fan-out and so very few disk accesses.
